Scientists traced the problem to deep, acidic water rising to the surface along the coast, and several businesses now monitor the water and add chemicals to protect their stock.

D  Because tiny shell-building plankton form the base of many ocean food webs, scientists worry that the effects could spread to fish and other animals that depend on them. Unlike warming, however, acidification can be addressed by only one solution on a global scale: reducing carbon dioxide emissions. Local measures, such as protecting seagrass meadows, which absorb carbon dioxide, may offer some limited relief in particular areas.

questions.q: The oceans take in about a ____ of the carbon dioxide released by humans each year.
questions.explain: A 段：absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide。take in = absorb。

questions.q: The absorption of carbon dioxide by the oceans has no benefits.
questions.explain: A 段：This slows the pace of global warming，减缓变暖就是好处，所以题干错误。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph B.
options: iii The value of oyster farming
questions.explain: B 段第一句：The change is particularly harmful to creatures that build shells or skeletons，后面讲为什么这些动物受害最重。

questions.q: What caused the oyster deaths in Oregon and Washington?
options: A Disease spread by imported oysters
B Acidic water coming up from the deep
questions.explain: C 段：deep, acidic water rising to the surface along the coast。D 是企业后来采取的保护措施，不是原因。

questions.q: Which paragraph explains why the problem may affect fish?
questions.explain: D 段：浮游生物是很多海洋食物网的基础，影响可能扩散到依赖它们的鱼类。

questions.q: Seagrass meadows can solve ocean acidification worldwide.
questions.explain: D 段：全球范围只有一个办法，就是减排；海草床只能在局部地区缓解（limited relief in particular areas）。题干的 worldwide 和原文矛盾。

title: How the Pyramids Were Built
text:
A  The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the pharaoh Khufu around 4,500 years ago, was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years. It originally stood about 146 metres high and contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone, most weighing between two and three tonnes.

B  The ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the pyramids were built by 100,000 slaves, and this image remained popular for centuries. However, archaeologists working at Giza since the 1990s have discovered the remains of a town where the workers lived, including bakeries, breweries and cemeteries. The way the workers were buried, close to the pyramids and with goods for the afterlife, suggests that they were paid labourers who were respected for their work.

C  How the heavy blocks were moved remains partly a mystery. Most limestone was quarried close to the site, but finer stone came from further away and granite was transported more than 800 kilometres by boat along the Nile. In 2013, archaeologists studying papyrus documents found the logbook of an official named Merer, who recorded transporting limestone blocks by boat to Giza.

D  Many researchers believe the blocks were raised using ramps of mud brick and rubble, although the exact design is still debated. A wall painting from another ancient site shows workers pouring water in front of a sledge carrying a large statue, and experiments have shown that wetting the sand in this way greatly reduces the force needed to pull a heavy load.

questions.q: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for almost four thousand years.
questions.explain: A 段：the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years。almost = nearly。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph B.
options: i New evidence about the workers
iv The size of the pyramid
questions.explain: B 段：希罗多德说是奴隶建的，但考古发现工人村和墓葬，说明他们是受尊重的有偿劳工。new evidence 对应 archaeologists ... have discovered。

questions.q: Archaeological evidence supports Herodotus's claim that slaves built the pyramids.
questions.explain: B 段：墓葬方式表明他们 were paid labourers who were respected，和奴隶说法相反。

questions.q: Granite was carried over 800 kilometres by ____ on the Nile.
questions.explain: C 段：granite was transported more than 800 kilometres by boat along the Nile。

questions.q: What did Merer's logbook record?
options: A The design of a ramp
B The transport of limestone to Giza
questions.explain: C 段：who recorded transporting limestone blocks by boat to Giza。

questions.q: Which paragraph mentions an experiment that tested an ancient method?
questions.explain: D 段：experiments have shown that wetting the sand ... greatly reduces the force needed。实验验证了壁画上往沙子上浇水的做法。

title: Too Many Tourists?
text:
A  International tourist arrivals grew from about 25 million in 1950 to almost 1.5 billion in 2019. Cheaper flights, rising incomes and the growth of online booking have made foreign travel possible for many more people, and tourism now accounts for a significant share of employment in countries such as Spain, Thailand and Greece.

B  In some popular destinations, however, residents complain of 'overtourism'. Venice, a city with fewer than 50,000 inhabitants in its historic centre, receives many millions of visitors a year. Locals say that crowds, rising rents and the replacement of ordinary shops by souvenir stores have made daily life difficult, and the population of the old city has fallen steadily for decades.

C  Short-term rental platforms have intensified the problem. When property owners can earn more by letting apartments to tourists than to long-term tenants, housing for local people becomes scarcer and more expensive. Barcelona has responded by refusing new licences for tourist flats and closing thousands of illegal ones.

D  Other places are experimenting with ways to manage visitor numbers. In 2024, Venice began charging day-trippers a fee to enter the city on its busiest days. Amsterdam has banned new hotels in its centre and runs campaigns discouraging certain types of visitors, and Bhutan has long required tourists to pay a substantial daily charge. Critics argue that such fees may turn travel into a privilege of the rich, while supporters say they protect places that would otherwise be damaged.

questions.q: International tourist numbers increased more than fifty times between 1950 and 2019.
questions.explain: A 段：从 2500 万涨到将近 15 亿，15 亿 ÷ 2500 万 = 60 倍，超过 50 倍。真题偶尔需要这样简单算一下。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a complaint by residents of Venice?
options: D Air pollution from cruise ships
questions.explain: B 段列了人多、房租上涨、普通商店变成纪念品店。邮轮污染原文没提。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i The effect of holiday rentals on housing
questions.explain: C 段讲短租平台让本地人的住房变少变贵。holiday rentals = short-term rental。

questions.explain: C 段：refusing new licences for tourist flats。stopped giving = refusing。注意英式拼写 licences。

questions.explain: D 段只说 2024 年开始在最忙的日子收费，没说效果如何。

title: Machines That Translate
text:
A  The idea of using computers to translate languages is almost as old as computers themselves. In 1954, researchers at Georgetown University and IBM demonstrated a system that translated more than 60 Russian sentences into English. The organisers predicted that machine translation would be a solved problem within a few years - a forecast that proved wildly optimistic.

B  Early systems relied on rules written by linguists, describing the grammar and vocabulary of each language. These worked reasonably well for simple, technical sentences, but struggled with ambiguity: a word such as 'bank' can mean the side of a river or a financial institution, and choosing correctly requires an understanding of context that rules could not easily capture.

C  From the 1990s, researchers turned to statistical methods, training programs on huge collections of texts that had already been translated by humans, such as the records of the Canadian parliament, which are published in both English and French. Since around 2016, systems based on artificial neural networks have produced far more fluent results, and they are now used by hundreds of millions of people every day.

D  Professional translators remain in demand, however. Machine translation still makes errors that a human would rarely make, especially with humour, cultural references and languages for which little translated text is available. In legal and medical documents, where a single mistake could have serious consequences, many organisations use machines to produce a first draft, which a human then checks and corrects.

questions.q: The prediction made in 1954 turned out to be accurate.
questions.explain: A 段：a forecast that proved wildly optimistic，预言过于乐观，没有实现。

questions.q: Why did rule-based systems have difficulty with the word 'bank'?
options: A It is not found in Russian.
B It has more than one meaning.
C It is a technical term.
questions.explain: B 段：bank 既可以是河岸也可以是银行，选对意思需要理解上下文。has more than one meaning = ambiguity。

questions.q: Statistical systems were trained using records of the Canadian ____, published in two languages.
questions.explain: C 段：such as the records of the Canadian parliament, which are published in both English and French。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i The limits of human translators
questions.explain: C 段讲统计方法和神经网络都是用人类已经翻好的大量文本来训练。iii 是 A 段，iv 是 B 段。

questions.q: Neural network translation is now used daily by very large numbers of people.
questions.explain: C 段：used by hundreds of millions of people every day。daily = every day。

questions.q: How do many organisations use machine translation for medical documents?
options: B They use it for a first version that a person then reviews.
C They use it only for humorous texts.
D They trust it more than human translators.
questions.explain: D 段：use machines to produce a first draft, which a human then checks and corrects。first draft = first version。

title: Power from Offshore Wind
text:
A  The world's first offshore wind farm was built in 1991 at Vindeby, off the coast of Denmark. It consisted of eleven turbines, each capable of generating 450 kilowatts. Modern offshore turbines are vastly larger: some now have a capacity of more than 15 megawatts, with blades over 100 metres long, and a single rotation can produce enough electricity to power an average home for a day.

B  Building turbines at sea has several advantages. Winds over the ocean are generally stronger and more consistent than on land, so offshore turbines generate electricity for a greater proportion of the time. They are also less likely to face objections from local residents about noise or the appearance of the landscape, although some coastal communities do oppose them.

C  The main drawback is cost. Turbines must be transported by specialist ships, fixed to the seabed and connected to the grid by long underwater cables, and maintenance in rough seas is expensive and sometimes dangerous. Most turbines stand on foundations fixed to the seabed, which limits them to waters less than about 60 metres deep. Floating turbines, anchored to the bottom by cables, could open up much deeper areas, but they remain at an early stage of development.

D  Despite these challenges, offshore wind has expanded rapidly. The United Kingdom generates a substantial share of its electricity from turbines in the North Sea, and China installed more offshore capacity in 2021 alone than the rest of the world had built in the previous five years. Environmental studies suggest that the foundations can even act as artificial reefs, attracting fish and other marine life.

questions.q: The Vindeby wind farm had more than ten turbines.
questions.explain: A 段：It consisted of eleven turbines。11 台，超过 10 台。

questions.q: According to paragraph B, why do offshore turbines produce electricity more often?
options: B Sea winds are stronger and steadier.
C They are closer to cities.
questions.explain: B 段：Winds over the ocean are generally stronger and more consistent。steadier = more consistent。D 是另一个优点，但不是“发电时间更长”的原因。

questions.q: No coastal communities object to offshore wind farms.
questions.explain: B 段末：although some coastal communities do oppose them。有些社区确实反对，题干说没有，所以是 FALSE。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
questions.explain: C 段第一句：The main drawback is cost，后面还讲了水深限制和浮式风机还不成熟。

questions.q: Turbines that are not fixed to the seabed but held by cables are called ____ turbines.
questions.explain: C 段：Floating turbines, anchored to the bottom by cables。

questions.q: Which paragraph mentions a possible benefit to sea creatures?
questions.explain: D 段末：the foundations can even act as artificial reefs, attracting fish and other marine life。

title: The Farming Ants
text:
A  Humans began farming around 12,000 years ago, but leafcutter ants have been cultivating crops for millions of years. Found in Central and South America, these ants cut pieces of leaves and carry them back to their underground nests. They do not eat the leaves. Instead, they use them to grow a fungus, which provides the colony's main source of food.

B  A mature colony can contain several million ants and is organised according to size. The largest workers, known as soldiers, defend the nest; medium-sized workers cut and carry the leaves; and the smallest workers tend the fungus gardens inside the nest, removing waste and chewing the leaf fragments into a pulp on which the fungus grows.

C  The ants must also protect their crop from disease. A particular mould can attack the fungus and destroy a garden. To fight it, the ants carry bacteria on their bodies that produce chemicals which kill the mould - a form of natural pesticide. Some researchers are studying these bacteria in the hope of discovering new antibiotics for human use.

D  Leafcutter ants have a significant effect on their environment. A single colony can harvest a large quantity of vegetation each year, and in some regions they are considered agricultural pests because they strip crops and trees. At the same time, by moving nutrients into the soil and creating underground tunnels, they help to recycle nutrients in rainforest ecosystems.

questions.q: Leafcutter ants feed on the leaves they collect.
questions.explain: A 段：They do not eat the leaves。它们不吃叶子，而是用叶子种真菌。

questions.q: What do the smallest workers do?
options: C Look after the fungus gardens
D Search for new nest sites
questions.explain: B 段：the smallest workers tend the fungus gardens。tend = look after。A 是兵蚁，B 是中等体型的工蚁。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i A natural defence against disease
ii How the colony is organised
v The size of ant nests
questions.explain: C 段讲蚂蚁身上的细菌能产生杀霉菌的化学物质，保护真菌不生病。ii 是 B 段的内容。

questions.q: Scientists hope the bacteria carried by the ants could lead to new ____.
questions.explain: C 段：in the hope of discovering new antibiotics for human use。

questions.q: Which paragraph describes both harmful and helpful effects of the ants?
questions.explain: D 段：在一些地方是农业害虫（harmful），同时又帮助雨林生态循环养分（helpful）。

questions.q: A leafcutter ant colony can survive for more than twenty years.
questions.explain: 全文没有提到蚁群能存活多久。题干的细节原文完全没出现，就是 NOT GIVEN。

title: Pen or Keyboard?
text:
A  For most of the twentieth century, students took notes by hand. Today, many arrive at lectures with laptops, which allow them to type faster and record more of what is said. It might seem obvious that taking more complete notes would lead to better learning, but a number of studies suggest that the situation is more complicated.

B  In a widely discussed study published in 2014, psychologists Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer asked students to watch recorded lectures and take notes either by hand or on a laptop. The laptop users wrote more words, but they were also more likely to copy the lecturer's sentences word for word. When tested later, the students who had written by hand performed better on questions that required understanding ideas rather than simply remembering facts.

C  The researchers suggested that because writing by hand is slower, it forces students to choose what is important and put it into their own words, a process that helps them understand and remember the material. Later attempts to repeat the study, however, produced smaller and less consistent differences, and some researchers argue that how students take notes matters more than the tool they use.

D  There is stronger evidence for the benefits of handwriting among young children. Studies of children learning to read have found that practising writing letters by hand, rather than typing them, helps them to recognise the letters more quickly. As a result, many education experts recommend that handwriting continue to be taught in primary schools, even as keyboards become more common.

questions.q: Laptops allow students to write down more of a lecture.
questions.explain: A 段：allow them to type faster and record more of what is said。

questions.q: What did the laptop users in the 2014 study tend to do?
options: B Copy the lecturer's exact words
questions.explain: B 段：more likely to copy the lecturer's sentences word for word。exact words = word for word。

questions.q: On which type of question did hand-writers perform better?
options: B Questions requiring understanding of ideas
questions.explain: B 段：performed better on questions that required understanding ideas rather than simply remembering facts。A 正是原文说的 rather than 后面的内容，是反向干扰。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i A possible explanation and later doubts
iii The design of the experiment
questions.explain: C 段前半讲研究者的解释（手写慢，迫使学生用自己的话总结），后半讲后来的重复研究差异更小、结果不一致（later doubts）。

questions.q: Later studies found an even larger advantage for handwriting.
questions.explain: C 段：produced smaller and less consistent differences。差异更小，题干说更大，所以是 FALSE。

questions.q: Many experts recommend that handwriting should still be taught in ____ schools.
questions.explain: D 段：handwriting continue to be taught in primary schools。

title: The Cycling City
text:
A  In Copenhagen, more people now travel to work or education by bicycle than by car. This was not always the case. In the 1960s and early 1970s, Danish cities, like many others in Europe, were redesigning their streets to accommodate rapidly growing car traffic, and cycling was in decline.

B  The oil crisis of 1973, when fuel prices rose sharply, prompted a change of direction. The Danish government introduced car-free Sundays to save fuel, and campaigners demanded safer streets for cyclists. Over the following decades, Copenhagen built an extensive network of cycle lanes, many of them physically separated from motor traffic by a raised kerb.

C  The city has continued to invest. It has constructed bridges exclusively for cyclists and pedestrians, and on some main routes the traffic lights are timed so that a cyclist riding at about 20 kilometres per hour can pass through a series of green lights without stopping. Official counts on one bridge have recorded more than 40,000 cyclists on a single day.

D  Supporters argue that the benefits extend well beyond transport. Cycling improves physical health, reduces air pollution and noise, and takes up far less space than driving. Studies in Denmark have estimated that each kilometre cycled saves society money once health benefits are taken into account. Other cities, including Paris, have recently tried to follow Copenhagen's example, although critics complain that new cycle lanes have increased congestion for drivers.

questions.q: Cycling in Copenhagen was becoming less common in the 1960s.
questions.explain: A 段：cycling was in decline。in decline = becoming less common。

questions.q: What led Denmark to change its transport policy in the 1970s?
options: A A rise in road accidents
B A sudden increase in fuel prices
questions.explain: B 段：The oil crisis of 1973, when fuel prices rose sharply, prompted a change of direction。prompted = led to。

questions.q: Many cycle lanes are separated from cars by a raised ____.
questions.explain: B 段：physically separated from motor traffic by a raised kerb。kerb 是英式拼写，美式写作 curb。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
questions.explain: C 段第一句：The city has continued to invest，后面举了自行车专用桥、绿波信号灯的例子。

questions.q: Copenhagen's traffic lights are timed to help cyclists travelling at around 20 km/h.
questions.explain: C 段：timed so that a cyclist riding at about 20 kilometres per hour can pass through a series of green lights。

questions.q: Which paragraph mentions an objection to building cycle lanes?
questions.explain: D 段末：critics complain that new cycle lanes have increased congestion for drivers。

title: The Hidden Network Beneath the Forest
text:
A  Beneath the floor of most forests lies a vast network of fungal threads. Many of these fungi form partnerships, called mycorrhizae, with the roots of trees and other plants. The fungi supply the plants with water and nutrients such as phosphorus from the soil, and in return the plants provide the fungi with sugars produced by photosynthesis. More than 90 percent of plant species are thought to form such relationships.

B  In the 1990s, the Canadian ecologist Suzanne Simard reported that carbon could pass between trees through these fungal connections. Her research, and that of others, led to the idea of a 'wood wide web', through which trees might share resources and even warn one another of insect attacks. Popular books presented a picture of forests as cooperative communities in which older 'mother trees' nourish their young.

C  In recent years, however, some scientists have questioned how strong the evidence is. A review published in 2023 argued that while fungal networks clearly exist, there is limited proof that they transfer significant amounts of resources between trees in natural forests, or that trees use them to help their offspring. The authors warned that popular accounts had gone further than the research justified.

D  The debate has practical importance. If fungal networks play a major role in forest health, forestry practices such as clearing all trees from an area may cause more harm than expected, because they destroy the networks along with the trees. Researchers on both sides agree that more field studies are needed, particularly in forests outside North America and Europe.

questions.q: What do plants give the fungi in a mycorrhizal partnership?
questions.explain: A 段：the plants provide the fungi with sugars。A 和 B 是真菌给植物的，方向别看反。

questions.q: Most plant species form partnerships with fungi.
questions.explain: A 段：More than 90 percent of plant species are thought to form such relationships。90% 以上就是 most。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph B.
options: i An attractive idea becomes popular
v The need for more studies
questions.explain: B 段：Simard 的研究催生了“树联网”的说法，畅销书把森林描述成互助社区。ii 是 C 段，v 是 D 段。

questions.q: The 2023 review denied that fungal networks exist.
questions.explain: C 段：while fungal networks clearly exist，综述承认网络存在，质疑的是它们传递资源的规模。

questions.q: The 2023 review said popular accounts had gone further than the ____ justified.
questions.explain: C 段：popular accounts had gone further than the research justified。

questions.q: Which paragraph explains why the debate matters for forest management?
questions.explain: D 段：The debate has practical importance，如果真菌网络很重要，把一片树全砍掉的林业做法可能危害更大。

title: The Problem of Food Waste
text:
A  According to the United Nations Environment Programme, around 1 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, roughly a fifth of all the food available to consumers. Households were responsible for the largest share, about 60 percent, with the rest wasted by restaurants, canteens and shops. Further losses occur earlier in the supply chain, on farms and during storage and transport.

B  The environmental cost is considerable. Producing food that is never eaten uses land, water and energy, and food that rots in landfill sites releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. It has been estimated that food loss and waste together account for between 8 and 10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

C  The causes differ between countries. In poorer nations, much food is lost before it reaches consumers because of inadequate storage facilities, refrigeration and roads. In wealthier countries, a greater proportion is thrown away by shops and households, often because of confusion over date labels: many people discard food that has passed its 'best before' date, even though this label refers to quality rather than safety.

D  A variety of solutions are being tried. Some supermarkets have removed 'best before' dates from fresh fruit and vegetables, and apps allow shops and restaurants to sell surplus food cheaply at the end of the day. France passed a law in 2016 that prohibits large supermarkets from destroying unsold food that is still fit to eat and requires them to donate it to charities instead.

questions.q: Households waste more food than restaurants, canteens and shops combined.
questions.explain: A 段：家庭约占 60%，剩下的 40% 才是餐馆、食堂和商店加起来，所以家庭更多。

questions.q: Food that decays in landfill produces ____, a strong greenhouse gas.
questions.explain: B 段：food that rots in landfill sites releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas。decays = rots。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i Different reasons in rich and poor countries
ii The cost to the environment
iv How to store food safely
v The size of the problem
questions.explain: C 段第一句：The causes differ between countries，然后分别讲穷国和富国。

questions.q: A 'best before' date indicates when food becomes unsafe to eat.
questions.explain: C 段：this label refers to quality rather than safety。它说的是品质，不是安全。

questions.q: What does the French law of 2016 require?
options: A Shops must sell food more cheaply.
B Large supermarkets must give edible unsold food to charities.
C Households must recycle food waste.
D Restaurants must use food apps.
questions.explain: D 段：requires them to donate it to charities instead。edible = fit to eat，give = donate。

questions.q: Food-sharing apps have greatly reduced food waste in France.
questions.explain: D 段提到了应用和法国的法律，但没说这些应用在法国的效果。

title: Science at the End of the Earth
text:
A  Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent on Earth. It has no permanent human population, but around 30 countries operate research stations there, housing several thousand scientists and support staff in summer and a much smaller number during the long, dark winter.

B  The continent is governed by the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 by twelve countries and since joined by more than 50 others. The treaty states that Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only, bans military activity and nuclear testing, and encourages scientific cooperation. A later agreement, which came into force in 1998, prohibits mining.

C  Antarctic research has produced major discoveries. In 1985, British scientists at Halley Research Station published evidence of a dramatic seasonal thinning of the ozone layer above the continent. This finding contributed to the Montreal Protocol of 1987, an international agreement to phase out the chemicals responsible, and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

D  Cores of ice drilled from deep within the ice sheet provide a record of the Earth's past climate. Tiny bubbles trapped in the ice contain samples of ancient air, allowing scientists to measure how levels of carbon dioxide have changed. The longest continuous core, drilled at a site called Dome C, covers around 800,000 years, and researchers are now drilling in search of ice more than a million years old.

questions.q: More people live in Antarctic research stations in winter than in summer.
questions.explain: A 段：several thousand ... in summer and a much smaller number during the long, dark winter。冬天人少得多。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT banned under the Antarctic Treaty system?
questions.explain: B 段：条约禁止军事活动和核试验，1998 年的协议禁止采矿，科研是被鼓励的。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: i A discovery that changed international policy
ii Life at a research station
iii The coldest place on Earth
v Countries that signed the treaty
questions.explain: C 段：英国科学家发现臭氧层变薄，促成了 1987 年的《蒙特利尔议定书》。international agreement = international policy。

questions.q: The ozone layer above Antarctica has now fully recovered.
questions.explain: C 段：the ozone layer is now slowly recovering，正在慢慢恢复，没有完全恢复。

questions.q: Small ____ in ice cores contain samples of ancient air.
questions.explain: D 段：Tiny bubbles trapped in the ice contain samples of ancient air。small = tiny。

questions.q: Which paragraph mentions an attempt to find even older material?
questions.explain: D 段末：researchers are now drilling in search of ice more than a million years old。

title: The Psychology of Colour
text:
A  Businesses spend large sums choosing the colours of their logos, products and packaging, based on the belief that colour influences how consumers feel and behave. Some marketing guides make confident claims: that red stimulates appetite, that blue suggests trustworthiness and that green signals environmental responsibility.

B  Scientific evidence for such fixed associations is weaker than these guides suggest. Reactions to colour vary according to culture, age and personal experience. White, for example, is associated with weddings and purity in many Western countries, but with mourning in parts of East Asia. Red, a symbol of good fortune in China, can signal danger or debt elsewhere.

C  What research does support is the importance of 'fit'. In studies where participants were shown brands in different colours, they responded more positively when the colour seemed appropriate to the product's personality. A colour that suits a children's toy may seem wrong for a bank or a luxury watch.

D  Colour can also help a brand stand out. Psychologists have long known that people remember items that differ from their surroundings, a principle sometimes called the isolation effect. Some companies have gone as far as seeking legal protection for a particular shade: a chocolate maker spent years in the courts trying to register a specific purple as its trademark, although its claim was ultimately rejected.

questions.q: Some marketing guides claim that blue makes a brand seem reliable.
questions.explain: A 段：blue suggests trustworthiness。reliable = trustworthy。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph B.
options: i Colours mean different things to different people
ii The cost of designing logos
iii Why red makes people hungry
questions.explain: B 段：人们对颜色的反应因文化、年龄、个人经历而不同，并举了白色和红色的例子。iii 是 A 段营销指南的说法，被 B 段质疑了。

questions.q: White is linked with sadness in parts of East Asia.
questions.explain: B 段：with mourning in parts of East Asia。mourning（哀悼）和 sadness 意思相关，这是真题常见的近义改写。

questions.q: According to paragraph C, when do people respond best to a brand's colour?
options: A When the colour is bright
B When it matches the character of the product
C When it is red or blue
D When it is the same as competitors' colours
questions.explain: C 段：when the colour seemed appropriate to the product's personality。matches the character = appropriate to the personality。

questions.q: People's tendency to remember things that differ from their surroundings is called the ____ effect.
questions.explain: D 段：a principle sometimes called the isolation effect。

questions.q: The chocolate maker succeeded in registering its purple as a trademark.
questions.explain: D 段：its claim was ultimately rejected，最后被驳回了。

title: Losing the Night Sky
text:
A  For most of human history, people could look up on a clear night and see thousands of stars and the bright band of the Milky Way. Today, according to a study published in 2016, more than a third of humanity, including around 80 percent of North Americans, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live, because artificial light makes the sky too bright.

B  Light pollution is not only a problem for astronomers. Many animals depend on natural patterns of light and darkness. Newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean by moving towards the brighter horizon over the water, but lights from coastal buildings can lead them inland, where they die. Migrating birds can become disoriented by brightly lit buildings, and millions are killed each year in collisions.

C  There may also be effects on human health. Exposure to light at night, particularly blue light, suppresses the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep. Some studies have found associations between night-time light and health problems, although it is difficult to separate the effects of light from other features of modern life.

D  Unlike many forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced quickly and cheaply. Shielding street lamps so that light is directed downwards, using warmer colours and switching off unnecessary lighting late at night can all make a significant difference. Several places have been certified as 'dark sky' areas, and in 2001 Flagstaff in Arizona became the world's first International Dark Sky City.

questions.q: Most North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from their homes.
questions.explain: A 段：around 80 percent of North Americans can no longer see the Milky Way。80% 就是 most。

questions.q: How do coastal lights harm young sea turtles?
options: A They make the water too warm.
B They lead the turtles away from the sea.
D They stop eggs from hatching.
questions.explain: B 段：lights from coastal buildings can lead them inland。inland = away from the sea。

questions.q: Choose the correct heading for paragraph C.
options: v The first dark sky city
questions.explain: C 段第一句：There may also be effects on human health。may 对应 possible。ii 是 B 段，iv、v 是 D 段。

questions.q: Light at night reduces the production of ____, which controls sleep.
questions.explain: C 段：suppresses the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep。reduces = suppresses，controls = regulates。

questions.q: Scientists have proved that night-time light directly causes serious illness.
questions.explain: C 段：只发现了相关性（associations），而且很难和现代生活的其他因素分开，所以不能说已经证明了直接导致。题干说 proved ... directly causes，和原文矛盾。

questions.q: Which paragraph states that this kind of pollution is easy to reduce?
questions.explain: D 段第一句：light pollution can be reduced quickly and cheaply。
